transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello, Ms. Williams. I'm Dr. Miller, the resident on the oncology team. I wanted to come in and talk with you personally about what happened with your infusion today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The nurse already told me. She said something went wrong with the date.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that's right. I want to be very clear about it. We gave you your immunotherapy dose on the wrong day of your cycle because of a calendar entry error. I am so sorry. I take full responsibility for this mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that even mean? Does it mean it didn't work?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It means the timing of the drug in your system isn't exactly where it needs to be for the maximum effect. Because it was given too early, there is a possibility it could reduce how effective this specific dose is.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't... I can't deal with this. I have two kids at home and I'm already working two jobs just to keep things floating while I'm sick. I can't be here longer than I have to.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you are feeling completely overwhelmed right now, and the pressure of taking care of your children while managing this is just too much.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is. My daughter is only four. If this treatment fails or if I have to stay here longer, who is going to actually pick her up from preschool? I'm terrified that this mistake just pushed my recovery back.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that fear.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You don't. You're not the one whose kids might not have a mom because a calendar was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're right, I'm not. I can't imagine the stress you're under trying to balance your jobs and your children while fighting this. I am truly sorry that our error has added to that burden.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? Do I just wait and see if the drug worked or not?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, we have a very specific plan to fix this. First, I have already consulted with the attending oncologist and our pharmacist. We are rescheduling your next dose to a modified date to get your cycle back on track. I will have that new date for you by 4:00 PM today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And the dose I already got?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are monitoring your blood work tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to see how your body is responding to the shifted timing. I'll be the one to call you with those results by noon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is this going to happen again? How do I know the next one is actually the right day?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a fair question. To prevent this from happening again, we've implemented a double-verification step. From now on, both the attending physician and the head nurse must sign off on the calendar date 48 hours before your infusion. You will also receive a confirmation text from us two days prior, so you can double-check the date with us before you even leave your house.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I guess that helps. I just... I'm so tired.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you are. We're going to move as quickly as possible to get this sorted so you can get back to your kids.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just hope this doesn't change everything.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can't promise the drug's effect won't be slightly altered, but I can promise that we are doing everything possible now to correct the course.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When did you say you'd have the new date?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: By 4:00 PM today. I'll come back in person to give it to you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll leave you alone for a bit so you can rest. I'll be back in a few hours.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts, remains regulated during the patient's pushback ('You don't'), and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the first turn using lay language, but there were no explicit checks for patient comprehension (e.g., 'Does that make sense?').

A.justification: The resident used direct apology language, took full responsibility ('I take full responsibility'), and maintained accountability when challenged.

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('overwhelmed', 'fear') and referenced the patient's specific life stressors regarding her children and jobs.

T.justification: The resident provided specific steps with timelines (4:00 PM today, 8:00 AM tomorrow), a patient role (double-checking the text), and a prevention plan.
